BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the result first (what it makes). 2) inputs and the place. 3) each step with its cause and its condition. 4) what breaks when a step fails. 5) the whole run once more at speed. 6) recap as a flow.
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the whole in context. 2) zoom into each part in a fixed path (outside to inside). 3) function of each part tied to its shape. 4) how the parts work together. 5) labelled recap.
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the basis of division first. 2) the tree from the top down. 3) each kind with its identifying feature and an example. 4) the borderline cases and exceptions. 5) the tree as recap.
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
  Teaching pattern: 1) what is common. 2) criteria one at a time, both sides together. 3) the reason behind each difference. 4) the most confused pair named directly. 5) difference table as recap.
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the period and its atmosphere. 2) events in order with their causes. 3) the people and their choices. 4) the turning point. 5) what changed after. 6) timeline recap.
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the effect students can see. 2) the cause. 3) each link of the chain with its mechanism. 4) the evidence. 5) the exception or limit. 6) the chain as recap.

  Teaching pattern: 1) a concrete example first. 2) the book's definition word by word. 3) a non-example that tests the boundary. 4) where the term is used next in the chapter.

Video v10: Plant-tissue tree और plant की growth वाली जगहें
Goal: पहले root, shoot, node, internode, leaf base, length और girth को plant outline पर दिखाएँगे। c05 के दोनों plant-tissue trees में हर split का basis बताकर top-down reading करेंगे; हर branch का identifying feature और source में दिया example पढ़ेंगे, जबकि detailed working आगे खोलेंगे। Meristematic cell को wall से cytoplasm, nucleus और vacuole तक पढ़कर active division से जोड़ेंगे। Apical, lateral और intercalary meristems को पूरे plant पर locate करके length और girth के असर समझाएँगे। c35 में हर location statement जाँचेंगे, खासकर root tips only वाले restrictive word को। Labelled plant और classification tree recap देंगे।
Opening hook: Plant लंबा भी होता है और उसका stem मोटा भी होता है। क्या दोनों काम एक ही जगह होते हैं?
Story or analogy: (none)
Planned minutes: 35
Prerequisites to teach first in this video (name · basis · why):
- Root, shoot, stem, leaf base, node, internode, bark, length and girth · outside · Outside basis: Locate plant growth regions and distinguish elongation from increased thickness; this prevents confusion between apical, intercalary and lateral meristems.

p001-i30 | 1 | diagram | classification | Classification of Plant Tissue → Meristematic Tissue and Permanent Tissue. Meristematic Tissue → Apical Meristem, Lateral Meristem, Intercalary Meristem. Permanent Tissue → Simple and Complex. Simple → Paranchyma, Collenchyma, Sclerenchyma. Sclerenchyma → Fibres and Sclereids. Complex → Xylem and Phloem. Visible Xylem components: Tracheids, Vessels (Tracheae), Xylem parenchyma. Visible Phloem components: Sieve tubes, Companion cells, Phloem parenchyma. The bottoms of the component boxes are cropped.
  p001-i30#q1 | which | Which main tissue groups and subgroups does the tree show? → Plant tissue divides into meristematic and permanent tissue. Meristematic tissue has apical, lateral and intercalary meristems; permanent tissue divides into simple and complex tissue, with further branches as shown. | book
  p001-i30#q2 | difference | What distinguishes the two main groups and the two permanent-tissue groups? → Meristematic cells actively divide; permanent tissues consist of cells differentiated for particular roles and generally no longer actively dividing. Simple tissues mainly contain one cell type, while complex tissues contain several cooperating cell types. | outside
  p001-i30#q3 | how | How should the connecting lines be read? → Read downward from a parent to its subtypes or listed components: Fibres and Sclereids belong under Sclerenchyma, while the lower conducting-cell lists belong under Xylem and Phloem respectively. | book
  p001-i30#q4 | why | Why is it important to distinguish levels in this tree? → Apical, lateral and intercalary are meristem types; fibres and sclereids are sclerenchyma forms; sieve tubes and companion cells are phloem components. Treating these labels as equivalent alternatives would lose their parent–child relationships. | book

  p001-i31#q1 | which | Which groups branch from the root? → Meristematic Tissue and Permanent Tissue. | book
  p001-i31#q2 | difference | What is the basis of their distinction? → Active division characterises meristematic tissue, while differentiation for particular functions characterises permanent tissue. | outside
  p001-i31#q3 | how | How does the root organise the chart? → All lower labels are reached through one of its two principal branches. | book

  p001-i32#q2 | difference | How does meristematic tissue differ from permanent tissue? → Meristematic tissue supplies actively dividing cells for growth; permanent tissue is differentiated for particular functions. | outside
  p001-i32#q3 | how | How does meristematic tissue support plant growth? → Its cells divide to add new cells, some of which subsequently enlarge and differentiate into permanent tissues. | outside

  p001-i33#q1 | which | Which main tissue group includes Apical Meristem? → Meristematic Tissue. | book
  p001-i33#q2 | difference | How does apical meristem differ in location and growth role from lateral meristem? → Apical meristems occur at root and shoot tips and support primary growth in length; lateral meristems occur along the sides and support growth in girth. | outside
  p001-i33#q3 | how | How does an apical meristem lengthen a root or shoot? → It produces new cells near the tip; subsequent cell elongation and differentiation contribute to extension. | outside

  p001-i34#q1 | which | Which branch contains Lateral Meristem? → The Meristematic Tissue branch. | book
  p001-i34#q2 | difference | How does lateral meristem differ from apical meristem? → Lateral meristems extend along the sides of stems or roots and contribute to thickness; apical meristems lie at tips and contribute to length. | outside
  p001-i34#q3 | how | How can lateral meristems increase girth? → Cambial tissues produce new cells toward the inside or outside, adding tissue layers around the organ. | outside

  p001-i35#q1 | which | Which category contains Intercalary Meristem? → Meristematic Tissue, alongside apical and lateral meristems. | book
  p001-i35#q2 | difference | How does intercalary meristem differ in position from apical meristem? → Intercalary meristems occur between more mature tissues, commonly near leaf bases or internode bases in grasses; apical meristems occur at growing tips. | outside
  p001-i35#q3 | how | How can intercalary meristems help grasses regrow after cutting? → Dividing cells at retained basal growth regions can continue producing new tissue even when upper portions have been removed. | outside

  p001-i36#q1 | which | Which two groups branch from Permanent Tissue? → Simple and Complex. | book
  p001-i36#q2 | difference | How is permanent tissue distinguished from meristematic tissue? → Permanent-tissue cells have differentiated for particular roles and generally ceased active division; meristematic cells retain active division. | outside
  p001-i36#q3 | how | How does permanent tissue arise? → Cells produced by meristems enlarge and differentiate, acquiring structures suited to roles such as support, storage or transport. | outside

  p001-i37#q1 | which | Which simple permanent tissues are listed? → Paranchyma, Collenchyma and Sclerenchyma, using the chart's spellings. | book
  p001-i37#q2 | difference | How does simple tissue differ from complex tissue? → Simple tissue consists mainly of one cell type, while complex tissue combines several cell types in a shared function. | outside
  p001-i37#q3 | why | Why are all three labels grouped under Simple? → Each is recognised as a tissue primarily characterised by one general type of cell, despite variations within that type. | outside

  p001-i38#q1 | which | Which complex tissues are shown? → Xylem and Phloem. | book
  p001-i38#q2 | difference | What distinguishes complex from simple permanent tissue? → Complex tissue contains different cell types working together, whereas simple tissue is mainly composed of one cell type. | outside
  p001-i38#q3 | how | How does the chart illustrate this complexity? → It lists several named components beneath each of Xylem and Phloem, showing that each includes multiple components. | book

  p001-i39#q1 | which | Which category contains the label Paranchyma? → Simple permanent tissue. | book
  p001-i39#q2 | difference | How does the tissue intended by this label differ from sclerenchyma? → The standard term is parenchyma. Its cells are generally living and have relatively thin primary walls; sclerenchyma commonly has thick lignified walls and cells dead at maturity. | outside
  p001-i39#q3 | how | How can parenchyma serve different functions? → Living cells can store materials, and chloroplast-containing forms can photosynthesise. Their functions depend on location and specialisation. | outside

  p001-i40#q1 | which | Where is Collenchyma classified? → Under Simple permanent tissue. | book
  p001-i40#q2 | difference | How does collenchyma differ from parenchyma? → Collenchyma has living cells with unevenly thickened primary walls suited to support, whereas typical parenchyma has relatively thin primary walls. | outside
  p001-i40#q3 | how | How does collenchyma support growing parts? → Its thickened but flexible walls provide strength while allowing bending and continued growth in young organs. | outside
p001-i41 | 1 | diagram_label | classification | Sclerenchyma: child of Simple under Permanent Tissue; parent of Fibres and Sclereids.
  p001-i41#q1 | which | Which two forms branch from Sclerenchyma? → Fibres and Sclereids. | book
  p001-i41#q2 | difference | How does sclerenchyma differ from collenchyma? → Sclerenchyma typically has thick lignified secondary walls and cells dead at maturity; collenchyma has living cells with unevenly thickened primary walls. | outside
  p001-i41#q3 | why | Why is sclerenchyma suited to mechanical strength? → Thick lignified walls resist deformation and reinforce mature plant parts. | outside

  p001-i42#q1 | which | Which tissue is the parent of Fibres here? → Sclerenchyma. | book
  p001-i42#q2 | difference | How do fibres generally differ from sclereids? → Fibres are usually long, narrow cells with tapering ends; sclereids are commonly shorter and more varied in shape. | outside
  p001-i42#q3 | how | How do fibres strengthen plant parts? → Their elongated, thick-walled cells often occur in groups and help resist pulling and bending forces. | outside
p001-i43 | 1 | diagram_label | classification | Sclereids: child of Sclerenchyma.
  p001-i43#q1 | which | Which parent tissue contains Sclereids? → Sclerenchyma, alongside Fibres. | book
  p001-i43#q2 | difference | How are sclereids distinguished from fibres? → Sclereids tend to be shorter or irregularly shaped, whereas fibres are characteristically elongated. | outside
  p001-i43#q3 | how | How do sclereids contribute to hardness? → Their thick lignified walls give local rigidity; stone cells in pear flesh provide a familiar example of their gritty texture. | outside
p001-i44 | 1 | diagram_label | classification | Xylem: child of Complex under Permanent Tissue. Visible listed components: Tracheids; Vessels (Tracheae); Xylem parenchyma. Lower box edge is cropped.
  p001-i44#q1 | which | Which visible components are listed under Xylem? → Tracheids, Vessels (Tracheae) and Xylem parenchyma. | book
  p001-i44#q2 | difference | How does xylem differ functionally from phloem? → Xylem chiefly transports water and mineral nutrients; phloem transports organic assimilates such as sugars between sources and sinks. | outside
  p001-i44#q3 | how | How can one complex tissue combine transport with other roles? → Different component cells specialise in conduction, storage or support. The visible crop should not be treated as an exhaustive list of xylem cell types. | outside
p001-i45 | 1 | diagram_label | classification | Tracheids: listed component of Xylem.
  p001-i45#q1 | which | Which tissue contains Tracheids in the chart? → Xylem, a complex permanent tissue. | book
  p001-i45#q2 | difference | How do tracheids differ from vessel elements? → Tracheids are elongated conducting cells without the perforation plates characteristic of vessel elements; water passes between tracheids through pits. | outside
  p001-i45#q3 | how | How are tracheids suited to water transport? → Their dead, hollow interiors permit water movement, while lignified walls provide support and help resist collapse under tension. | outside
p001-i46 | 1 | diagram_label | classification | Vessels (Tracheae): listed component of Xylem.
  p001-i46#q1 | which | Which tissue contains Vessels (Tracheae)? → Xylem. | book
  p001-i46#q2 | difference | How do vessels differ from individual tracheids? → Vessels consist of vessel elements joined end to end through perforated end walls, forming extended conducting channels; tracheids conduct between cells through pits. | outside
  p001-i46#q3 | how | How does this arrangement assist water flow? → The connected lumens and perforated end walls provide a relatively open route along the vessel. | outside
p001-i47 | 1 | diagram_label | classification | Xylem parenchyma: listed component of Xylem.
  p001-i47#q1 | which | Which complex tissue includes Xylem parenchyma? → Xylem. | book
  p001-i47#q2 | difference | How does xylem parenchyma differ from mature tracheids and vessel elements? → Xylem parenchyma cells are living, whereas mature tracheids and vessel elements are dead conducting cells. | outside
  p001-i47#q3 | how | How does living parenchyma contribute to xylem? → It stores materials and assists lateral movement and exchange of substances within the tissue. | outside
p001-i48 | 1 | diagram_label | classification | Phloem: child of Complex under Permanent Tissue. Visible listed components: Sieve tubes; Companion cells; Phloem parenchyma. Lower box edge is cropped.
  p001-i48#q1 | which | Which visible components are listed under Phloem? → Sieve tubes, Companion cells and Phloem parenchyma. | book
  p001-i48#q2 | difference | How does phloem transport differ from xylem transport? → Phloem mainly carries organic assimilates from sources to sinks, whereas xylem mainly carries water and mineral nutrients. | outside
  p001-i48#q3 | how | How do different phloem cell types cooperate? → Sieve-tube elements provide conducting pathways, companion cells support their metabolism and transport processes, and parenchyma contributes storage and exchange. | outside
p001-i49 | 1 | diagram_label | classification | Sieve tubes: listed component of Phloem.
  p001-i49#q1 | which | Which complex tissue contains Sieve tubes? → Phloem. | book
  p001-i49#q2 | difference | How do sieve-tube elements differ from xylem vessel elements? → Mature sieve-tube elements are living conducting cells that lack a nucleus in angiosperms; mature xylem vessel elements are dead and have lignified walls. | outside
  p001-i49#q3 | how | How do sieve tubes form a transport route? → Sieve-tube elements join end to end, with sieve-plate pores allowing phloem sap to pass between them. | outside
p001-i50 | 1 | diagram_label | classification | Companion cells: listed component of Phloem.
  p001-i50#q1 | which | Which tissue includes Companion cells? → Phloem. | book
  p001-i50#q2 | difference | How do companion cells differ from mature sieve-tube elements? → Companion cells retain nuclei and dense metabolically active contents; mature sieve-tube elements lose their nuclei and are specialised for conduction. | outside
  p001-i50#q3 | why | Why are companion cells closely associated with sieve-tube elements? → They provide metabolic support and participate in loading, unloading and maintaining the conducting system through close cellular connections. | outside
p001-i51 | 1 | diagram_label | classification | Phloem parenchyma: listed component of Phloem.
  p001-i51#q1 | which | Which complex tissue contains Phloem parenchyma? → Phloem. | book
  p001-i51#q2 | difference | How does phloem parenchyma differ in role from sieve tubes? → Phloem parenchyma mainly contributes storage and local exchange, while sieve tubes specialise in long-distance transport of phloem sap. | outside
  p001-i51#q3 | how | How does parenchyma support the functioning of phloem? → Its living cells store substances and help move materials laterally between conducting tissue and surrounding cells. | outside
p008-i10 | 8 | diagram | classification | Plant Tissues branches into Meristematic tissue and Permanent tissue. Meristematic tissue branches into Apical meristem, Intercalary meristem and Lateral meristem. Permanent tissue branches into Simple permanent tissue and Complex permanent tissue. Simple permanent tissue branches into Parenchyma, Collenchyma and Sclerenchyma. Parenchyma branches into Aerenchyma and Chlorenchyma. Sclerenchyma branches into Sclerenchyma fibers and Sclereids. Complex permanent tissue branches into Xylem and Phloem. Connecting lines and downward arrows show classification relationships, not a temporal sequence.
  p008-i10#q1 | which | Which are the main divisions and further branches of plant tissues? → Plant tissues divide into meristematic and permanent tissues. Meristematic tissue includes apical, intercalary and lateral meristems. Permanent tissue includes simple and complex tissues. Simple tissues include parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma; parenchyma includes aerenchyma and chlorenchyma, and sclerenchyma includes fibers and sclereids. Complex tissues include xylem and phloem. | book
  p008-i10#q2 | difference | What distinguishes the major categories in this tree? → Meristematic tissue contains actively dividing cells involved in growth. Permanent tissues contain differentiated cells with specialised roles. Simple permanent tissues have one main cell type, whereas complex permanent tissues contain different cell types working together. | outside
  p008-i10#q3 | how | How should a student read the branching arrows? → Follow a line from a parent category to its subcategories. For example, phloem belongs to complex permanent tissue, which belongs to permanent tissue, which belongs to plant tissues. | book
p008-i11 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Plant Tissues — root label; branches to Meristematic tissue and Permanent tissue.
  p008-i11#q1 | which | Which two categories lie immediately below Plant Tissues? → Meristematic tissue and Permanent tissue. | book
  p008-i11#q2 | difference | What basic distinction separates these categories? → Meristematic tissues are regions of active cell division; permanent tissues consist of differentiated cells specialised for particular functions. | outside
  p008-i11#q3 | why | Why does a plant need both kinds? → It needs new cells for growth and specialised cells for functions such as support, photosynthesis and transport. | outside
p008-i12 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Meristematic tissue — child of Plant Tissues; parent of Apical meristem, Intercalary meristem and Lateral meristem.
  p008-i12#q1 | which | Which meristems are shown under meristematic tissue? → Apical, intercalary and lateral meristems. | book
  p008-i12#q2 | difference | How do these three meristems differ? → They differ by position: apical meristems occur at growing tips, intercalary meristems occur between mature tissue regions, and lateral meristems occur along the sides of stems and roots. | outside
  p008-i12#q3 | how | How do meristems contribute to growth? → Their cells divide to produce new cells, which can enlarge and differentiate into tissues. | outside
p008-i13 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Apical meristem — child of Meristematic tissue.
  p008-i13#q1 | which | Which tissue category contains apical meristem? → Meristematic tissue. | book
  p008-i13#q2 | difference | How does apical meristem differ from lateral meristem? → Apical meristem occurs at root and shoot tips and contributes to length growth; lateral meristem occurs along the sides and contributes to increased girth. | outside
  p008-i13#q3 | how | How does activity at a tip increase plant length? → Cell division produces new cells near the tip, and subsequent cell enlargement extends the root or shoot. | outside
p008-i14 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Intercalary meristem — child of Meristematic tissue.
  p008-i14#q1 | which | Which group contains intercalary meristem? → Meristematic tissue. | book
  p008-i14#q2 | difference | How does an intercalary meristem differ in position from an apical meristem? → An intercalary meristem occurs between mature tissue regions, often at the bases of internodes or leaves in grasses, rather than at the terminal growing tip. | outside
  p008-i14#q3 | how | How can intercalary meristems help grasses regrow after cutting? → Basal dividing regions may remain after upper parts are removed and produce cells that support renewed elongation. | outside
p008-i15 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Lateral meristem — child of Meristematic tissue.
  p008-i15#q1 | which | Which category contains lateral meristem? → Meristematic tissue. | book
  p008-i15#q2 | difference | How does lateral meristem differ from apical meristem in growth contribution? → Lateral meristems contribute to increased thickness or girth, whereas apical meristems contribute to length growth. | outside
  p008-i15#q3 | how | How does a lateral meristem increase girth? → Dividing cells in layers along the sides add new tissue, increasing the diameter of the stem or root. | outside
p008-i16 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Permanent tissue — child of Plant Tissues; parent of Simple permanent tissue and Complex permanent tissue.
  p008-i16#q1 | which | Which two groups lie under permanent tissue? → Simple permanent tissue and Complex permanent tissue. | book
  p008-i16#q2 | difference | How do permanent and meristematic tissues differ? → Permanent tissue cells have differentiated for particular functions and generally do not actively divide; meristematic cells actively divide to produce new cells. | outside
  p008-i16#q3 | how | How do permanent tissues arise? → Cells produced by meristems enlarge and differentiate, acquiring structures suited to specialised functions. | outside
p008-i17 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Simple permanent tissue — child of Permanent tissue; parent of Parenchyma, Collenchyma and Sclerenchyma.
  p008-i17#q1 | which | Which simple permanent tissues are shown? → Parenchyma, Collenchyma and Sclerenchyma. | book
  p008-i17#q2 | difference | What distinguishes simple from complex permanent tissue? → A simple permanent tissue has one main kind of cell; a complex permanent tissue contains different kinds of cells working together. | outside
  p008-i17#q3 | why | Why does 'simple' not mean functionally unimportant? → It describes cellular composition. Simple tissues perform major roles such as storage, photosynthesis and support. | outside
p008-i18 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Complex permanent tissue — child of Permanent tissue; parent of Xylem and Phloem.
  p008-i18#q1 | which | Which complex permanent tissues are shown? → Xylem and Phloem. | book
  p008-i18#q2 | difference | How does complex tissue differ from simple tissue? → Complex tissue combines different cell types in a common functional system; simple tissue is composed mainly of one cell type. | outside
  p008-i18#q3 | how | How do different cell types help a transport tissue work? → Some cells form conducting pathways, while others provide support, storage or assistance to transport. | outside
p008-i19 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Parenchyma — child of Simple permanent tissue; parent of Aerenchyma and Chlorenchyma.
  p008-i19#q1 | which | Which subtypes are linked to parenchyma? → Aerenchyma and Chlorenchyma. | book
  p008-i19#q2 | difference | How does parenchyma generally differ from sclerenchyma? → Parenchyma generally consists of living cells with relatively thin primary walls. Mature sclerenchyma cells generally have thick, lignified walls and are dead. | outside
  p008-i19#q3 | how | How can parenchyma perform different functions? → Its living cells may store materials, contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis or be arranged with large air spaces, producing functional specialisations. | outside
p008-i20 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Collenchyma — child of Simple permanent tissue.
  p008-i20#q1 | which | Which category contains collenchyma? → Simple permanent tissue. | book
  p008-i20#q2 | difference | How does collenchyma differ from sclerenchyma? → Collenchyma has living cells with unevenly thickened primary walls and provides flexible support. Sclerenchyma generally has dead mature cells with thick, lignified walls and provides more rigid support. | outside
  p008-i20#q3 | how | How can collenchyma support a growing plant part? → Its strengthened but relatively flexible walls resist mechanical stress while permitting growth and bending. | outside
p008-i21 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Sclerenchyma — child of Simple permanent tissue; parent of Sclerenchyma fibers and Sclereids.
  p008-i21#q1 | which | Which two forms of sclerenchyma are shown? → Sclerenchyma fibers and Sclereids. | book
  p008-i21#q2 | difference | How do these forms differ? → Fibres are typically long and narrow; sclereids are generally shorter and occur in varied shapes. | outside
  p008-i21#q3 | why | Why is sclerenchyma suited to mechanical support? → Its thick, lignified cell walls resist deformation and strengthen plant parts. | outside
p008-i22 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Aerenchyma — child of Parenchyma.
  p008-i22#q1 | which | Which tissue is the parent of aerenchyma? → Parenchyma. | book
  p008-i22#q2 | difference | How does aerenchyma differ from chlorenchyma? → Aerenchyma is characterised by large air spaces; chlorenchyma is characterised by chloroplast-containing cells suited to photosynthesis. | outside
  p008-i22#q3 | how | How do the air spaces help plants in aquatic or waterlogged conditions? → They facilitate internal gas movement and can contribute to buoyancy in aquatic plant parts. | outside
p008-i23 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Chlorenchyma — child of Parenchyma.
  p008-i23#q1 | which | Which parent tissue contains chlorenchyma? → Parenchyma. | book
  p008-i23#q2 | difference | What distinguishes chlorenchyma from aerenchyma? → Chlorenchyma contains chloroplasts for photosynthesis, whereas aerenchyma has prominent air spaces. | outside
  p008-i23#q3 | how | How do chloroplasts enable chlorenchyma to make food? → Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll that captures light energy for photosynthesis, allowing cells to form carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water. | outside
p008-i24 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Sclerenchyma fibers — child of Sclerenchyma.
  p008-i24#q1 | which | Which tissue contains sclerenchyma fibers? → Sclerenchyma, a simple permanent tissue. | book
  p008-i24#q2 | difference | How do sclerenchyma fibers differ from sclereids? → Fibres are typically elongated and narrow, while sclereids are generally shorter and have varied shapes. | outside
  p008-i24#q3 | how | How do fibres strengthen plant parts? → Their elongated form and thick, lignified walls, often arranged in bundles, help resist pulling and bending forces. | outside
p008-i25 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Sclereids — child of Sclerenchyma.
  p008-i25#q1 | which | Which tissue category contains sclereids? → Sclerenchyma. | book
  p008-i25#q2 | difference | How do sclereids differ from sclerenchyma fibers? → Sclereids generally have shorter, varied shapes, whereas fibres are typically long and narrow. | outside
  p008-i25#q3 | why | Why can sclereids make plant parts hard or gritty? → Their very thick, lignified walls form hard cells; such cells contribute to hard coverings and the gritty texture of pear flesh. | outside
p008-i26 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Xylem — child of Complex permanent tissue.
  p008-i26#q1 | which | Which category contains xylem? → Complex permanent tissue. | book
  p008-i26#q2 | difference | How does xylem differ functionally from phloem? → Xylem mainly transports water and dissolved minerals from roots towards aerial parts; phloem transports organic food from sources to regions that use or store it. | outside
  p008-i26#q3 | how | How is xylem suited to water transport? → Its conducting elements form pathways for water, and their strengthened walls help resist collapse under the tension associated with transpiration. | outside
p008-i27 | 8 | diagram_label | classification | Phloem — child of Complex permanent tissue.
  p008-i27#q1 | which | Which category contains phloem? → Complex permanent tissue. | book
  p008-i27#q2 | difference | How does phloem transport differ from xylem transport? → Phloem carries organic food from sources to sinks, while xylem mainly carries water and minerals from roots towards aerial parts. | outside
  p008-i27#q3 | how | How can phloem transport serve both growing roots and developing fruits? → Both can act as sinks that use or store sugars. Phloem connects food-producing or food-releasing sources with these sinks. | outside
p009-i3 | 9 | list_point | structure | • OCCURRENCE: Growing region of plant like root, shoot etc.
  p009-i3#q1 | what | What tissue is associated with the growing regions of a plant? → Meristematic tissue occurs in growing regions, including regions of roots and shoots. | book
  p009-i3#q2 | where | Does the page place meristematic tissue throughout the entire root and shoot? → It places the tissue in growing regions of these organs; the later subtype descriptions identify root and shoot tips, regions beneath bark, and bases of leaves or internodes. | book
  p009-i3#q3 | why | Why do growing regions require meristematic tissue? → Growth requires a supply of new cells. Meristematic cells divide to supply cells that can subsequently enlarge and specialise. | outside
p009-i4 | 9 | list_point | structure | • Shape: Spherical, oval/rectangular.
  p009-i4#q1 | what | Which shapes does the page list for meristematic cells? → It lists spherical, oval and rectangular shapes. | book
  p009-i4#q2 | where | Which cells does this shape description apply to? → It applies to the cells making up meristematic tissue in plant growing regions. | book
  p009-i4#q3 | how | How should these shapes be used when identifying meristematic tissue? → Shape should be considered with other features, such as compact arrangement and active cell division. A cell's outline alone does not establish that it is meristematic. | outside
p009-i5 | 9 | list_point | cause_effect | • Intercellular spaces: Absent, hence compactly packed.
  p009-i5#q1 | why | Why does the page describe meristematic cells as compactly packed? → It states that intercellular spaces are absent, so there are no spaces separating the neighbouring cells in the tissue. | book
  p009-i5#q2 | how | How does absence of intercellular spaces affect tissue arrangement? → Neighbouring cells lie closely against one another, producing a compact arrangement. | book
  p009-i5#q3 | difference | How is an intercellular space different from a vacuole? → An intercellular space lies between cells, whereas a vacuole is a compartment within a cell. Absence of one does not mean the same thing as absence of the other. | outside
p009-i6 | 9 | list_point | structure | • Vacuoles absent in it.
  p009-i6#q1 | what | What does the page state about vacuoles in meristematic tissue? → The page states that vacuoles are absent. | book
  p009-i6#q2 | where | Where would a vacuole be located if present? → A vacuole is a membrane-bound compartment within the cell, rather than a gap between adjacent cells. | outside
  p009-i6#q3 | why | Why are large vacuoles generally not a prominent feature of meristematic cells? → Actively dividing cells typically have dense cytoplasm and lack the large central vacuole characteristic of many mature plant cells. Small vacuoles may occur, so the page's statement is an introductory simplification. | outside
p009-i7 | 9 | list_point | process | • Focus only on cell division.
  p009-i7#q1 | what | What principal activity does the page assign to meristematic cells? → The page emphasises cell division as their principal activity. | book
  p009-i7#q2 | how | How does cell division contribute to plant growth? → Division increases cell number. The new cells can enlarge and differentiate, contributing to growth and the formation of specialised tissues. | outside
  p009-i7#q3 | when | When is this dividing activity associated with growth? → It occurs while meristematic regions are active during plant growth; particular meristems may be less active or dormant under some conditions. | outside
  p009-i7#q4 | exception | Does 'focus only on cell division' mean the cells perform no other cellular activities? → No. It highlights their growth-producing role. Dividing cells also carry out metabolism and make the materials needed for division. | outside
p009-i8 | 9 | list_point | facts_numbers | • Highly active cells.
  p009-i8#q1 | what | How does the page describe meristematic cell activity? → It describes meristematic cells as highly active. | book
  p009-i8#q2 | evidence | Which other statement on the page supports this description? → The preceding bullet emphasises cell division, identifying the growth-related activity being highlighted. | book
  p009-i8#q3 | why | Why does active division require considerable cellular activity? → A cell preparing to divide must copy its genetic material, produce cellular components and use energy to form daughter cells. | outside
p008-i28 | 8 | diagram | structure | A small upright shoot sketch shows a pointed growing tip, leaves at successive stem levels and highlighted growth regions. Apical meristem points to the shoot tip; Intercalary meristem points to a highlighted transverse region near a leaf base; Lateral meristem points to the longitudinal side region of the stem. The sketch locates meristems spatially rather than showing a sequence.
  p008-i28#q1 | what | What does the small shoot sketch show? → It shows the positions of apical, intercalary and lateral meristems on a shoot. | book
  p008-i28#q2 | where | Where are the three meristems marked? → Apical meristem is at the shoot tip, intercalary meristem is at a transverse region near a leaf base, and lateral meristem is along the side of the stem. | book
  p008-i28#q3 | how | How does their position relate to growth? → Apical and intercalary meristems contribute to elongation in their respective regions, while lateral meristems contribute to increased thickness. | outside
p008-i29 | 8 | diagram_label | structure | Apical meristem — points to the growing tip of the shoot.
  p008-i29#q1 | what | What does the top label identify? → Apical meristem. | book
  p008-i29#q2 | where | Where does its pointer end? → At the shoot's terminal growing tip. | book
  p008-i29#q3 | how | How does this region help extend the shoot? → It produces new cells by division; subsequent cell enlargement contributes to shoot elongation. | outside
p008-i30 | 8 | diagram_label | structure | Intercalary meristem — points to a highlighted transverse region of the shoot near a leaf base, below the terminal tip.
  p008-i30#q1 | what | What region does the side label identify? → Intercalary meristem. | book
  p008-i30#q2 | where | Where is the intercalary region shown? → As a transverse highlighted region near a leaf base, below the shoot tip. | book
  p008-i30#q3 | how | How does an intercalary meristem produce local elongation? → Dividing cells at the base of an internode or leaf produce new cells that enlarge, extending that region. | outside
p008-i31 | 8 | diagram_label | structure | Lateral meristem — points to the longitudinal side region of the stem.
  p008-i31#q1 | what | What does the label beneath the shoot identify? → Lateral meristem. | book
  p008-i31#q2 | where | Where is lateral meristem marked? → Along a side region of the stem rather than at the tip. | book
  p008-i31#q3 | how | How does division in this position affect the stem? → It adds tissue along the sides and contributes to an increase in stem girth. | outside

  p009-i9#q1 | what | What relationship does the whole-plant drawing show? → It connects the positions of apical, intercalary and lateral meristems with the regions in which a plant grows. | book
  p009-i9#q2 | which | Which visual elements distinguish elongation from thickening? → The blue arrows extend along the shoot-root axis, while the paired orange arrows point outward at the stem. | book
  p009-i9#q3 | how | How should the arrow directions be interpreted? → The blue arrows illustrate extension in length at root and shoot tips. The orange arrows illustrate the increase in girth associated with lateral meristem. | book
p009-i10 | 9 | diagram_label | figure | Shoot: labels the small shoot-tip inset.
  p009-i10#q1 | what | What does the 'Shoot' label identify? → It identifies the small inset showing a shoot tip. | book
  p009-i10#q2 | which | Which meristem is associated with this tip? → The apical meristem is associated with the shoot tip. | book
  p009-i10#q3 | how | How does activity here contribute to shoot growth? → Division supplies new cells near the shoot apex; subsequent cell enlargement contributes to shoot elongation. | outside
p009-i11 | 9 | diagram_label | figure | Apical Meristem: the upper callout points to the shoot tip of the main plant.
  p009-i11#q1 | what | What does the upper 'Apical Meristem' callout identify? → It identifies the meristem at the shoot tip. | book
  p009-i11#q2 | which | Which growth effect belongs to this meristem? → Increase in shoot length belongs to the apical meristem. | book
  p009-i11#q3 | why | Why is the meristem called apical? → 'Apical' refers to an apex or tip, matching its position at the end of the shoot. | outside
p009-i12 | 9 | diagram_label | figure | Node: labels the node region in the enlarged green segment beside the plant.
  p009-i12#q1 | what | What label appears on the enlarged green segment? → The segment is labelled 'Node'. | book
  p009-i12#q2 | which | Which meristem is illustrated beside this node-related inset? → The nearby callout identifies intercalary meristem. | book
  p009-i12#q3 | how | How can a student distinguish a node from an internode? → A node is the region of a stem where a leaf attaches; an internode is the stem segment between successive nodes. This distinction is needed to interpret the page's intercalary growth statements. | outside
p009-i13 | 9 | diagram_label | figure | Intercalary Meristem: points to the region near a leaf attachment on the stem, beside the node inset.
  p009-i13#q1 | what | What does the 'Intercalary Meristem' label identify? → It identifies a meristematic region near a leaf attachment, within the length of the shoot. | book
  p009-i13#q2 | which | Which textual location should be associated with this callout? → The text places intercalary meristem at the base of leaves or internodes. | book
  p009-i13#q3 | how | How does this position differ from an apical meristem's position? → It lies between more mature regions along the organ, whereas an apical meristem is at a root or shoot apex. | outside
p009-i14 | 9 | diagram_label | figure | Lateral Meristem: points to the side of the stem, next to the cylindrical stem inset.
  p009-i14#q1 | what | What region does the lateral meristem callout identify? → It identifies a region along the side of the stem. | book
  p009-i14#q2 | which | Which growth direction should be paired with this label? → The outward orange arrows and increase in girth should be paired with lateral meristem. | book
  p009-i14#q3 | why | Why does a side-positioned meristem contribute to thickening? → Lateral meristems produce cells in arrangements that add tissue to the root or stem's thickness. | outside
p009-i15 | 9 | diagram_label | figure | Stem: labels a green cylindrical inset with a highlighted layer along its outer side.
  p009-i15#q1 | what | What does the cylindrical inset represent? → It represents the stem and highlights a layer near its outside. | book
  p009-i15#q2 | which | Which meristem is this inset used to illustrate? → It illustrates lateral meristem. | book

frame.process: Classify plant tissues by active division, cellular composition and the identifying features of lower branches.
frame.how: Read both trees from parent to child; distinguish tissue types, specialised forms and components.
frame.when: Read the main division first, then meristem types, permanent-tissue groups and their lower branches; arrows are not a time sequence.
frame.conditions: Use textbook explanations to interpret labels; preserve spelling differences and acknowledge cropped component lists.
frame.atmosphere: Two branching plant-tissue charts beside a simple plant outline.

frame.process: Locate meristematic tissue and examine the cells that supply new cells for growth.
frame.how: Move from growing regions to cell outlines, then wall, cytoplasm, nucleus and the vacuole position.
frame.when: Inspect the whole growing region before zooming into its cells.
frame.conditions: Identify cells using a combination of features; qualify the book's statement that vacuoles are absent.
frame.atmosphere: A plant growing region enlarged into a labelled textbook cell sketch.

frame.process: Explain the compact arrangement of meristematic cells.
frame.how: Absent intercellular spaces mean neighbouring cells lie closely together.
frame.when: Observe the compact tissue first, then trace the explanation back to spaces between cells.
frame.conditions: Intercellular spaces are outside cells; vacuoles are inside cells and require a separate description.
frame.atmosphere: Adjacent cell outlines with the between-cell and within-cell locations highlighted separately.

frame.process: Active meristematic cells divide to supply new cells for plant growth.
frame.how: Cells prepare for division, divide and supply descendants that may enlarge and differentiate.
frame.when: The sequence operates during active meristem growth; activity can decrease or become dormant.
frame.conditions: Division needs energy, materials and genetic preparation; division alone does not describe every aspect of growth.
frame.atmosphere: A growing tip shown beside a simplified sequence of cell division and later cell development.

frame.process: Interpret the book's qualitative description of meristematic cells as highly active.
frame.how: Link the description to division, genetic copying, component production and energy use.
frame.when: Read this description after understanding what active division involves.
frame.conditions: The page supplies no numerical division rate or activity measurement.
frame.atmosphere: The two book statements about division and high activity shown together.

frame.process: Locate the 3 meristems and connect each position with elongation or increased girth.
frame.how: Move from tips to leaf or internode bases and then to the lateral region beneath bark.
frame.when: Locate the whole plant first, inspect each region, then combine their growth effects.
frame.conditions: Intercalary growth depends on a retained active basal region; lateral thickening applies where lateral meristems operate.
frame.atmosphere: A whole plant and the small shoot sketch with distinct length and girth indicators.

frame.process: Read the whole-plant and enlarged-shoot figures as maps of meristem positions and growth effects.
